analysis.one_liner: Ends federal income tax on Social Security benefits, paid for by taxing wages above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, up to 85% of a retiree's Social Security check can be taxed as income. This bill would remove Social Security benefits from federal income tax entirely. To make up the lost money, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to every dollar of wages above $250,000 (currently, wages above about $168,600 are exempt), with a small corresponding benefit increase for those high earners. The bill also protects Social Security trust funds from losing revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and disability beneficiaries who currently pay federal income tax on part of their Social Security benefits — roughly the middle- and upper-middle-income retirees who cross the taxation thresholds. The Social Security trust funds also gain revenue from taxing earnings above the $250,000 threshold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Excludes Social Security benefits from gross income for federal income tax purposes, ending the taxation of benefits for all recipients
Funds this by removing the cap so Social Security payroll taxes apply to wages and self-employment income above $250,000, after 2024
Holds the Social Security and Medicare trust funds harmless by appropriating an amount equal to any revenue lost from the tax change

Extends a modest benefit formula (2% of excess earnings) to high earners' wages above $250,000, so newly taxed earnings count toward benefits, and protects SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries from benefit increases that could reduce their eligibility

analysis.who_pays: People with wages or self-employment income above $250,000 per year, who would pay Social Security payroll tax (6.2% for employees, 6.2% for employers, 12.4% for the self-employed) on the portion above that threshold, and their employers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers earning over $250,000 and their employers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes on earnings above $250,000, a direct cost increase for high earners, the self-employed above that level, and employers who pay the matching share

Extending the tax above the cap while paying benefits on those earnings changes Social Security's traditional link between taxes paid and benefits received, which critics of such proposals argue weakens the program's contributory character

Because no committee reported the bill, it never received analysis or amendments in the ordinary legislative process, so practical questions like compliance costs for multi-employer workers under the new tax were never examined

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is straightforward and deliberate: a tax cut for Social Security recipients paid for by higher payroll taxes on income above $250,000. The bill tries to soften objections by crediting high earners with a small benefit increase on their newly taxed earnings and protecting the trust funds. The main unresolved issue is that it never advanced far enough for anyone to score or refine it in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and the House never considered it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on January 25, 2024, with original cosponsors including Ro Khanna, Yadira Caraveo, Don Davis, Mary Peltola, Andrea Salinas, and Hillary Scholten
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction
It received subcommittee referrals — to Health in January 2024, and to Work and Welfare and Social Security in December 2024 — but no committee or subcommittee took it up
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without a floor vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above $250,000 keep the current payroll tax cap, and status quo taxation of Social Security benefits continues. Retirees who would have benefited saw no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners; retirees saw no change

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized its cosponsorship

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup during the two-year Congress

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor calendar in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans holding the House majority, no committee or floor action followed.

industries.industry: High-income households (wages and self-employment income above $250,000)
industries.note: They would pay Social Security payroll tax on all income above $250,000, offset by a small benefit credit on those earnings. The bill died, so the current cap stayed in place.
Employers pay a matching 6.2% Social Security tax on wages above the current cap; the bill would have extended that to pay up to $250,000 per employee.
